learningPoint: A urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 in PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia points to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, a benign condition in which parathyroidectomy must be avoided.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has a six-month history of episodic severe headache, palpitations, profuse sweating and pallor lasting about 20 minutes, occurring several times a week and sometimes provoked by bending or exercise. During an episode in clinic her blood pressure is 186/104 mmHg; between episodes it is 142/88 mmHg. Plasma free metanephrines are elevated more than three-fold above the upper limit of normal on two occasions. CT of the abdomen demonstrates a 4 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units. Potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.0), glucose 7.9 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Arrange laparoscopic adrenalectomy within the next week without additional medication
explanation: The paroxysmal triad of headache, palpitations and sweating with episodic hypertension, biochemical confirmation with raised plasma free metanephrines (the most sensitive test) and an adrenal mass with high unenhanced attenuation establish the diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumour of adrenal chromaffin cells. Definitive treatment is surgical excision, but operating on an unprepared patient risks a hypertensive crisis during tumour manipulation and profound hypotension after removal. Preoperative preparation therefore begins with alpha-adrenergic blockade, traditionally with the non-competitive, non-selective alpha-blocker phenoxybenzamine (or the selective alpha-1 antagonist doxazosin), titrated over 10 to 14 days to control blood pressure and allow re-expansion of the contracted intravascular volume, with liberal salt and fluid intake. Only once alpha-blockade is established is a beta-blocker added to control reflex tachycardia. Starting a beta-blocker first is dangerous: unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, with loss of beta-2 vasodilatation, can precipitate a hypertensive crisis and acute heart failure. Further workup includes functional imaging (MIBG or PET) to exclude extra-adrenal or metastatic disease, and genetic testing because up to 40% are hereditary (RET in MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHB and SDHD). Hyperglycaemia is common because catecholamines suppress insulin release.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: surgery without adequate alpha-blockade risks intraoperative hypertensive crisis and postoperative circulatory collapse.
Incorrect: beta-blockade before alpha-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.
Correct: alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine (or doxazosin) for 10 to 14 days is the essential first step before surgery.
Incorrect: ACE inhibitors do not block catecholamine effects and are not the recommended preoperative agent.
Incorrect: spironolactone treats primary hyperaldosteronism, which is excluded by the normal potassium and raised metanephrines.
learningPoint: Phaeochromocytoma requires alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) before beta-blockade and surgery; never start a beta-blocker first.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with 12 months of abdominal bloating, intermittent loose stools and persistent fatigue. Her sister has type 1 diabetes. Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115–165), MCV 74 fL (80–100), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (15–200), folate 2.1 micrograms/L (>3.0). IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody 145 U/mL (<7) with a normal total IgA. She has read about coeliac disease online and is keen to start a gluten-free diet straight away. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a gluten-free diet now and repeat serology in six months
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsies while she continues to eat gluten
explanation: Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Iron and folate deficiency with gastrointestinal symptoms, and a first-degree relative with an associated autoimmune condition, are typical. NICE guidance (NG20) recommends serological testing with IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (with total IgA to exclude selective IgA deficiency, in which IgG-based tests are needed) as the first-line investigation, but in adults a positive serology must be confirmed by duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh classification) before a lifelong diagnosis is made. Crucially, both serology and histology normalise on a gluten-free diet, so patients must continue to eat gluten in more than one meal a day for at least six weeks before testing. Starting the diet now would risk a false-negative biopsy and a missed or uncertain diagnosis, with implications for lifelong dietary restriction, prescription of gluten-free products, osteoporosis screening, family screening and vaccination against pneumococcus (hyposplenism). HLA typing has a high negative predictive value and is useful when the diagnosis is unclear or the patient is already gluten-free, but it cannot confirm the disease because around 30% of the population carry these alleles.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: colonoscopy investigates colonic disease; the diagnostic lesion of coeliac disease is in the proximal small bowel.
Incorrect: faecal calprotectin screens for inflammatory bowel disease and does not diagnose coeliac disease.
Incorrect: HLA typing can exclude but cannot confirm coeliac disease because these alleles are common in the general population.
Incorrect: starting a gluten-free diet before biopsy normalises histology and serology, making definitive diagnosis impossible.
Correct: adults with positive serology need duodenal biopsy on a gluten-containing diet to confirm the diagnosis.
learningPoint: Confirm coeliac disease in adults with duodenal biopsy while the patient is still eating gluten; a gluten-free diet before biopsy leads to false-negative results.

stem: A 34-year-old nurse who was born in Vietnam and moved to the United Kingdom five years ago attends an occupational health appointment before starting work in an endoscopy unit. She is asymptomatic and has never knowingly had jaundice. She does not recall receiving hepatitis B vaccination. Serology: HBsAg negative; anti-HBs 1,100 mIU/mL (positive above 10); anti-HBc total (IgG) positive; anti-HBc IgM negative; HBeAg negative; anti-HBe positive; HBV DNA undetectable. ALT 22 U/L (<40). Which of the following best describes her hepatitis B status?
options: Immunity from previous hepatitis B vaccination
Resolved past hepatitis B infection with natural immunity
explanation: Interpreting hepatitis B serology depends on three key markers. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) indicates current infection, whether acute or chronic (chronic if it persists beyond six months). Antibody to core antigen (anti-HBc) indicates exposure to the virus itself and never results from vaccination, because the vaccine contains only recombinant surface antigen; IgM anti-HBc indicates recent (acute) infection, while IgG anti-HBc persists for life. Antibody to surface antigen (anti-HBs) indicates immunity, either from vaccination (in which case anti-HBc is negative) or from resolved natural infection (anti-HBc positive). This woman is HBsAg negative with positive anti-HBs and IgG anti-HBc, negative IgM, undetectable DNA and normal ALT, which is the classic pattern of a resolved past infection with natural immunity, common in people born in areas of high endemicity where perinatal or childhood transmission occurs. Anti-HBe with negative HBeAg is consistent with this. She does not require vaccination or antiviral therapy and poses no infection risk to patients, though she should be counselled that reactivation can occur with profound immunosuppression (for example rituximab or chemotherapy), when antiviral prophylaxis is considered. Occult infection would show detectable HBV DNA despite negative HBsAg.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: acute infection would show HBsAg positive with IgM anti-HBc and usually raised ALT.
Incorrect: an inactive carrier remains HBsAg positive with low or undetectable DNA and normal ALT.
Incorrect: vaccine-induced immunity produces anti-HBs alone; anti-HBc is never positive after vaccination.
Incorrect: occult infection is defined by detectable HBV DNA in the absence of HBsAg; her DNA is undetectable.
Correct: negative HBsAg with positive anti-HBs and IgG anti-HBc indicates cleared past infection with natural immunity.
learningPoint: Anti-HBc positivity means past exposure to hepatitis B virus (never from vaccination); with negative HBsAg and positive anti-HBs it indicates resolved infection with natural immunity.

stem: A 26-year-old man with known left-sided ulcerative colitis is admitted with nine bloody stools per day, abdominal cramps, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius and heart rate 104/min. Haemoglobin 101 g/L (130–180), CRP 68 mg/L (<5), albumin 28 g/L (35–50). Stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin are negative and abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation. He is started on intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily, low molecular weight heparin and intravenous fluids. On day 3 he still has seven bloody stools per day, CRP is 52 mg/L and he remains tachycardic. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue intravenous hydrocortisone alone and reassess on day 7
explanation: He meets Truelove and Witts criteria for acute severe ulcerative colitis (six or more bloody stools daily plus at least one of temperature above 37.8, pulse above 90, haemoglobin below 105 g/L or ESR/CRP above 30). First-line treatment is intravenous corticosteroids together with prophylactic anticoagulation, fluid and electrolyte replacement and exclusion of infection, with joint medical and surgical review. Response should be formally assessed on day 3: the Oxford (Travis) criteria of more than eight stools per day, or three to eight stools with a CRP above 45 mg/L, predict an 85% likelihood of colectomy on that admission, and indicate that rescue therapy or surgery is needed rather than continuing steroids alone. NICE (NG130) recommends adding intravenous ciclosporin (2 mg/kg) to steroids when there is little or no improvement within 72 hours, or infliximab if ciclosporin is contraindicated or unsuitable; the two are equally effective (CONSTRUCT trial). Failure to respond to rescue therapy within 4 to 7 days, or deterioration, toxic megacolon, perforation or haemorrhage at any stage, mandates colectomy. Azathioprine takes months to act and mesalazine is ineffective in acute severe disease. Ciclosporin requires monitoring of blood pressure, renal function, magnesium and cholesterol.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: oral aminosalicylates have no role in the acute management of severe colitis.
Incorrect: failure to respond by day 3 predicts a high colectomy risk and prolonging steroids alone delays effective treatment.
Correct: rescue therapy with intravenous ciclosporin (or infliximab) is indicated when there is inadequate response to intravenous steroids after 72 hours.
Incorrect: azathioprine is a maintenance agent with a slow onset and is not used for acute rescue.
Incorrect: colectomy is indicated if rescue therapy fails or complications develop; it is not yet mandated in a stable patient without dilatation.
learningPoint: In acute severe ulcerative colitis, assess response on day 3; more than eight stools or three to eight stools with CRP above 45 mg/L indicates the need for rescue ciclosporin or infliximab with surgical review.

stem: A 54-year-old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis and previous ascites is brought to the emergency department after two episodes of large-volume haematemesis. Heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, drowsy but responding to voice. Haemoglobin 82 g/L (130–180), platelets 76 x 10^9/L (150–400), INR 1.9 (0.8–1.2), bilirubin 68 micromol/L (<21), albumin 26 g/L (35–50). Two large-bore cannulae are inserted, blood products are given via the major haemorrhage protocol and the endoscopist is on the way. Which of the following should be administered before endoscopy?
options: Intravenous terlipressin and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
Platelet transfusion to achieve a count above 100 x 10^9/L
explanation: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding in a patient with cirrhosis should be presumed variceal until proven otherwise. NICE guidance (CG141) and BSG guidelines recommend that terlipressin, a vasopressin analogue that causes splanchnic vasoconstriction and reduces portal pressure, is given at presentation to all patients with suspected variceal bleeding and continued until haemostasis is achieved or for up to five days; it reduces bleeding and improves survival. Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics (for example intravenous co-amoxiclav or a third-generation cephalosporin according to local policy) should also be given at presentation because bacterial infection, particularly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, occurs in up to 50% of cirrhotic patients with variceal bleeding and antibiotics reduce rebleeding, infection and mortality. Endoscopy should be performed within 12 hours (immediately after resuscitation in unstable patients), with band ligation for oesophageal varices and cyanoacrylate injection for gastric varices; transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is used for uncontrolled bleeding. Restrictive transfusion to a haemoglobin target of 70 to 80 g/L improves outcomes, while over-transfusion raises portal pressure. Proton pump inhibitors have no proven pre-endoscopy benefit and tranexamic acid was shown in HALT-IT to increase thromboembolic events without reducing mortality. Non-selective beta-blockers are for secondary prophylaxis once stable.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: pre-endoscopy proton pump inhibitors are not recommended by NICE and do not treat variceal bleeding.
Correct: terlipressin lowers portal pressure and prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and death in cirrhotic patients with variceal bleeding.
Incorrect: the HALT-IT trial showed tranexamic acid does not reduce mortality in gastrointestinal bleeding and increases venous thromboembolism.
Incorrect: oral propranolol is for secondary prophylaxis after recovery, not during acute haemorrhage with hypotension.
Incorrect: routine platelet transfusion is not indicated at a count of 76 and does not correct the coagulopathy of liver disease.
learningPoint: Suspected variceal bleeding: give terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation, resuscitate with a restrictive transfusion strategy, and perform endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours.

stem: A 47-year-old man of Irish descent is investigated for fatigue, reduced libido and pain in the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands. He drinks 10 units of alcohol per week. He has a slate-grey complexion and 3 cm of smooth hepatomegaly. Ferritin 1,450 micrograms/L (30–400), transferrin saturation 78% (20–50), ALT 62 U/L (<40), fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L, testosterone low with low gonadotrophins. Genetic testing shows homozygosity for the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene. Liver stiffness on transient elastography is 6.8 kPa (normal). Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Venesection at regular intervals until iron stores are depleted
explanation: Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder of iron overload, most commonly due to homozygosity for the C282Y mutation in HFE, which impairs hepcidin production and leads to unrestrained intestinal iron absorption. Iron deposits in the liver (cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma), pancreas (bronze diabetes), pituitary (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism), joints (a characteristic arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints with chondrocalcinosis), heart (cardiomyopathy) and skin (pigmentation). Screening is with transferrin saturation (the earliest abnormality, above 45 to 50%) and ferritin, followed by HFE genotyping. The treatment of choice is therapeutic venesection: each 450 to 500 mL unit removes about 200 to 250 mg of iron, and weekly venesection is continued until ferritin is below 50 micrograms/L and transferrin saturation below 50%, followed by maintenance venesection every two to four months. Venesection prevents progression, improves fatigue and skin changes and can improve cardiac function, though established cirrhosis, diabetes and arthropathy may not reverse. Iron chelation is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate venesection, for example because of anaemia or cardiac failure. Dietary iron restriction alone is insufficient, though vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish (Vibrio vulnificus risk) should be avoided. First-degree relatives should be screened, and patients with cirrhosis need six-monthly ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: oral chelators are second-line for patients in whom venesection is contraindicated or not tolerated.
Incorrect: desferrioxamine is used for transfusional iron overload or when venesection is impossible, not as first-line in haemochromatosis.
Incorrect: dietary measures alone cannot remove the accumulated iron burden.
Incorrect: ursodeoxycholic acid treats primary biliary cholangitis and has no role in iron overload.
Correct: weekly venesection until ferritin is below 50 micrograms/L, then maintenance, is the standard treatment for hereditary haemochromatosis.
learningPoint: Hereditary haemochromatosis (HFE C282Y homozygosity, raised transferrin saturation and ferritin) is treated with venesection to a ferritin below 50 micrograms/L; screen first-degree relatives.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis secondary to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis presents with two days of diffuse abdominal discomfort, worsening ascites and mild confusion. Temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg. Diagnostic paracentesis: neutrophil count 480 cells/mm3 (<250), total protein 9 g/L, culture pending. Bilirubin 62 micromol/L (<21), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60–110; baseline 84), sodium 129 mmol/L (135–145), INR 1.8 (0.8–1.2), albumin 24 g/L (35–50). Intravenous cefotaxime is started. In addition to antibiotics, which intervention has been shown to reduce mortality in this situation?
explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is diagnosed when the ascitic fluid neutrophil count exceeds 250 cells/mm3 in the absence of a surgical source; culture is positive in only about 40% of cases. It carries a high mortality, largely through precipitation of hepatorenal syndrome and further hepatic decompensation. Bacterial translocation and the inflammatory response cause splanchnic vasodilatation, reduced effective circulating volume and renal hypoperfusion. A landmark randomised trial (Sort et al., 1999) and subsequent studies showed that intravenous human albumin solution, given as 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 together with a third-generation cephalosporin, reduces the incidence of renal impairment from around 30% to 10% and lowers in-hospital mortality from 29% to 10%. The benefit is greatest in patients with a raised creatinine (above 88 micromol/L), a bilirubin above 68 micromol/L, or a urea above 10.7 mmol/L, all of which mark high risk, and BSG and EASL guidelines recommend albumin in these patients. After recovery, long-term secondary prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin is recommended because recurrence is about 70% within a year, and patients should be assessed for liver transplantation. Diuretics and large-volume paracentesis worsen circulatory dysfunction and renal perfusion in active SBP, and non-selective beta-blockers are usually withheld in SBP with hypotension or renal impairment.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: diuretics further deplete effective circulating volume and precipitate hepatorenal syndrome during SBP.
Correct: albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces renal failure and mortality in SBP, especially with raised creatinine or bilirubin.
Incorrect: large-volume paracentesis during active infection worsens circulatory dysfunction and is not a mortality-reducing intervention here.
Incorrect: lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy but has not been shown to reduce mortality in SBP.
Incorrect: non-selective beta-blockers should generally be withheld in SBP with hypotension or acute kidney injury because they impair renal perfusion.
learningPoint: In spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, intravenous albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) with antibiotics reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality, particularly when creatinine or bilirubin is raised.

stem: An 82-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease, treated with co-beneldopa, is admitted with a urinary tract infection and started on antibiotics. On the second night he becomes acutely agitated, with fluctuating attention and disorganised thinking; he is trying to climb over the bed rails, has pulled out his cannula twice and is striking out at staff. Reorientation, reassurance, a quiet side room, the presence of his daughter and correction of hypoxia and pain have not settled him, and he is at immediate risk of serious injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological option?
explanation: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition precipitated by a physical cause, here infection in a vulnerable brain. NICE guidance (CG103) emphasises identifying and treating the cause, non-pharmacological de-escalation and environmental measures, and reserves drug treatment for patients who are distressed or a risk to themselves or others when verbal and non-verbal techniques have failed. In most patients short-term low-dose haloperidol is the first-line drug, but antipsychotics that block dopamine D2 receptors (haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine) are contraindicated in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, where they cause severe worsening of parkinsonism, falls, neuroleptic sensitivity reactions and increased mortality. In these patients a short-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam 0.5 mg (oral or intramuscular) is the recommended alternative, used at the lowest dose for the shortest time, with monitoring for respiratory depression and paradoxical agitation. If an antipsychotic is unavoidable in Parkinson's disease, quetiapine at low dose is the least likely to worsen motor function. Anticholinergic sedatives such as promethazine worsen confusion. Dopaminergic medication should be continued, as omission can itself precipitate delirium and neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: haloperidol is a potent D2 antagonist and is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease because it severely worsens parkinsonism.
Correct: a low-dose short-acting benzodiazepine is the recommended option for dangerous agitation in delirium when antipsychotics are contraindicated, as in Parkinson's disease.
Incorrect: olanzapine blocks D2 receptors and worsens motor function in Parkinson's disease.
Incorrect: promethazine is strongly anticholinergic and sedating and worsens delirium.
Incorrect: risperidone has potent D2 antagonism and is unsuitable in Parkinson's disease.
learningPoint: For delirium requiring sedation in Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia, avoid antipsychotics and use low-dose lorazepam; treat the underlying cause first.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is referred after her third fall in six months, each occurring within a minute of standing up from a chair or getting out of bed, with light-headedness beforehand but no loss of consciousness, chest pain or palpitations. She takes amlodipine 10 mg, doxazosin 4 mg, bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg, amitriptyline 25 mg at night for sleep and zopiclone 7.5 mg. Lying blood pressure 146/84 mmHg; standing blood pressure at three minutes 112/68 mmHg with reproduction of symptoms. Heart rate 72/min regular, ECG normal, cognition intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
explanation: Her falls are caused by orthostatic hypotension, defined as a fall in systolic blood pressure of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic 10 mmHg or more) within three minutes of standing, with symptoms reproduced. NICE guidance on falls in older people (CG161) recommends that anyone with recurrent falls receives a multifactorial falls risk assessment, and medication review is the intervention with the strongest evidence and lowest risk. She is taking five drugs that cause or aggravate orthostatic hypotension and falls: two antihypertensives that lower standing pressure (doxazosin, an alpha-blocker, is a particularly potent cause), a diuretic that reduces volume, a tricyclic with alpha-blocking and anticholinergic effects, and a hypnotic that impairs balance and cognition. Deprescribing should start with the alpha-blocker, the diuretic and the sedatives, using tools such as STOPP/START, with reassessment of blood pressure targets in the context of frailty (NICE suggests measuring standing pressure and treating to the standing value in people with postural hypotension). Non-pharmacological measures include slow staged standing, adequate fluid and salt intake, compression stockings and head-up tilt at night. Fludrocortisone and midodrine are reserved for persistent symptomatic orthostatic hypotension after culprit drugs are withdrawn. Imaging is not indicated without head injury or focal signs, and hip protectors have poor adherence and modest evidence.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: fludrocortisone is used only when orthostatic hypotension persists after removing causative drugs, and it worsens hypertension and oedema.
Incorrect: midodrine is a specialist-initiated option after reversible causes have been addressed.
Incorrect: hip protectors do not prevent falls, have weak evidence for fracture prevention and are poorly tolerated.
Correct: medication review and withdrawal of culprit drugs is the first and most effective intervention for drug-induced orthostatic hypotension.
Incorrect: CT head is not indicated for falls with a clear haemodynamic cause and no head injury or neurological signs.
learningPoint: Recurrent falls with a postural drop demand a structured medication review first; alpha-blockers, diuretics, tricyclics and hypnotics are common culprits.

stem: A 77-year-old woman sustains a distal radius fracture after tripping on a kerb. DXA scanning shows a T-score of minus 2.9 at the femoral neck and minus 3.1 at the lumbar spine. She has a long-standing benign peptic oesophageal stricture with intermittent dysphagia to solids, and is unable to remain upright for more than a few minutes after eating because of kyphosis. Adjusted calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m2 (>90). Dental examination is satisfactory. Which of the following is the most appropriate bone-protective treatment?
options: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone
Oral alendronic acid 70 mg once weekly
explanation: A fragility fracture with a DXA T-score at or below minus 2.5 confirms osteoporosis, and treatment is indicated to reduce the high risk of further fractures, particularly of the hip and spine. NICE and NOGG guidance recommend oral bisphosphonates (alendronate or risedronate) as first-line, but they are contraindicated in patients with oesophageal abnormalities such as strictures or achalasia, and in those who cannot remain upright for at least 30 minutes after a dose, because of the risk of severe oesophagitis and ulceration. This woman has both contraindications. Intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg given as a once-yearly infusion is the appropriate alternative (NICE TA464 supports it for patients in whom oral bisphosphonates are unsuitable); it reduces vertebral, non-vertebral and hip fractures and improves survival after hip fracture. Renal function must be above 35 mL/min and vitamin D should be replete to avoid hypocalcaemia; an acute-phase reaction after the first infusion is common. Denosumab is another option when bisphosphonates are unsuitable, but requires uninterrupted six-monthly dosing because of rebound vertebral fractures on cessation. Calcium and vitamin D alone do not adequately reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis. Hormone replacement therapy is not recommended for osteoporosis in women over 60 because of cardiovascular and breast cancer risk, and raloxifene reduces only vertebral fractures and increases thromboembolic risk.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: calcium and vitamin D are adjuncts and insufficient alone after a fragility fracture with osteoporotic T-scores.
Correct: annual intravenous zoledronic acid is recommended when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated by oesophageal disease or inability to remain upright.
Incorrect: oral alendronate is contraindicated with an oesophageal stricture and inability to remain upright for 30 minutes.
Incorrect: HRT is not recommended for osteoporosis in a 77-year-old because of breast cancer, stroke and thromboembolic risks.
Incorrect: raloxifene reduces only vertebral fractures, increases venous thromboembolism and is a lesser option than parenteral bisphosphonate.
learningPoint: Oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated with oesophageal disease or inability to stay upright for 30 minutes; use yearly intravenous zoledronic acid (or denosumab) instead.

stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson's disease of 9 years duration, taking co-beneldopa 25/100 four times daily and no other dopaminergic medication, is admitted with aspiration pneumonia. A speech and language therapy assessment finds an unsafe swallow and he is made nil by mouth. Two attempts to place a nasogastric tube fail and he is unable to tolerate further attempts. His last dose of co-beneldopa was five hours ago and he is becoming increasingly rigid and hypophonic. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to maintain his antiparkinsonian therapy?
options: Omit dopaminergic medication until his swallow recovers
Sublingual crushed co-beneldopa despite nil-by-mouth status
Transdermal rotigotine patch at a dose equivalent to his levodopa
explanation: Patients with Parkinson's disease must not have their dopaminergic medication abruptly interrupted. Missed doses cause rapid deterioration in mobility, swallowing and speech, increase the risk of aspiration, pressure damage and falls, prolong admission and, in severe cases, precipitate parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome (an acute akinetic state resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity, fever, autonomic instability and raised creatine kinase, which carries significant mortality). NICE guidance (NG71) and Parkinson's UK stress that medication should be given on time, and when the oral route is unavailable and a nasogastric tube cannot be placed, the dopamine agonist rotigotine, delivered as a 24-hour transdermal patch, is the standard alternative. Conversion calculators (for example the OPTIMAL calculator) convert the total daily levodopa equivalent dose into a rotigotine dose, usually capped at 16 mg per 24 hours, with the patch started immediately. Subcutaneous apomorphine is an alternative but requires specialist supervision and prior domperidone. Intravenous levodopa is not available in routine UK practice. Anticholinergics such as procyclidine do not replace dopaminergic therapy and cause confusion in older people. Crushing tablets and giving them orally to a patient with an unsafe swallow risks further aspiration, and dispersible co-beneldopa still requires swallowing.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: anticholinergics have minimal effect on bradykinesia, do not substitute for levodopa and cause delirium in older adults.
Incorrect: intravenous levodopa is not available for routine clinical use in the UK.
Incorrect: omitting dopaminergic therapy causes rapid deterioration and risks parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome.
Incorrect: giving oral medication to a patient with an unsafe swallow risks aspiration and is contrary to nil-by-mouth status.
Correct: a transdermal rotigotine patch, dosed using a levodopa-equivalent conversion, maintains dopaminergic stimulation when oral and enteral routes are unavailable.
learningPoint: Never abruptly stop Parkinson's medication; if the patient is nil by mouth and enteral access is impossible, convert to a transdermal rotigotine patch using a levodopa-equivalent calculator.

stem: An 84-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's dementia is admitted with a displaced intracapsular fracture of the neck of femur after a fall at home. She refuses surgery, saying she wants to go home. When the orthopaedic team explain the fracture, the operation and the consequences of not operating in simple language on several occasions, she cannot recall what the operation is for, repeatedly states that the doctors are making it up, and cannot describe what would happen without treatment. There is no evidence of delirium. Her daughter holds a registered Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare and, having discussed it with the team, supports surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Apply to the Court of Protection before any treatment is given
Detain her under Section 2 of the Mental Health Act to enable surgery
Discharge her home with community follow-up as she requests
Proceed with surgery in her best interests, with the attorney's consent, having documented that she lacks capacity for this decision
Respect her refusal as a valid autonomous decision and manage the fracture conservatively
explanation: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) sets out that capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and must be presumed unless shown to be lacking. A person lacks capacity if, because of an impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain, they are unable to understand information relevant to the decision, retain it long enough to decide, use or weigh it, or communicate their decision, after all practicable steps to help them have been taken. This woman cannot understand, retain or weigh the information despite repeated simple explanation and there is an underlying impairment (dementia), so she lacks capacity for this decision. A decision must then be made in her best interests, considering her past and present wishes, involving those close to her, and choosing the least restrictive option. A registered health and welfare Lasting Power of Attorney gives the attorney legal authority to consent to or refuse treatment on her behalf once she lacks capacity (unless the LPA excludes life-sustaining treatment decisions), so the daughter can lawfully consent. Hip fracture surgery is the least restrictive effective option, since conservative management carries high mortality, immobility and pain. The Mental Health Act cannot be used to authorise treatment for physical illness. The Court of Protection is reserved for disputes or particularly serious decisions where no one has authority.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: an application to the Court is unnecessary when a registered attorney can consent and there is no dispute.
Incorrect: the Mental Health Act authorises treatment of mental disorder only, not orthopaedic surgery.
Incorrect: discharging a patient who lacks capacity with an untreated hip fracture would not be in her best interests.
Correct: she lacks capacity for this decision, so treatment proceeds in her best interests with the consent of the health and welfare attorney.
Incorrect: a refusal is only autonomous if the person has capacity; she does not, so it cannot be treated as a valid refusal.
learningPoint: Capacity is decision-specific: if a patient cannot understand, retain, weigh or communicate, act in their best interests, respecting a registered health and welfare LPA's authority to consent.

stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to clinic by his wife with 18 months of progressive cognitive decline. His alertness and abilities vary markedly from day to day, with some days when he seems almost normal. He describes well-formed, detailed visual hallucinations of children playing in the house, which he knows are not real. His wife reports that he shouts and thrashes his limbs during sleep as if acting out dreams. He has had two unexplained falls. Examination shows mild bradykinesia, rigidity and a reduced arm swing without tremor. MMSE 22/30 with prominent visuospatial and attentional deficits but relatively preserved memory. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease and is caused by alpha-synuclein aggregation in cortical and subcortical neurons. The consensus diagnostic criteria (McKeith 2017) define core clinical features: fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder (which often precedes cognitive decline by years) and one or more spontaneous features of parkinsonism. This patient has all four. Supportive features include repeated falls, syncope, autonomic dysfunction, severe sensitivity to antipsychotics and prominent visuospatial and executive dysfunction with relatively preserved memory early on. Indicative biomarkers are reduced dopamine transporter uptake on DaT-SPECT, low uptake on cardiac MIBG scintigraphy and polysomnographic confirmation of REM sleep without atonia. By convention, if dementia begins within a year of parkinsonism the diagnosis is DLB; if parkinsonism precedes dementia by more than a year it is Parkinson's disease dementia. Management is important: antipsychotics can cause severe, sometimes fatal, neuroleptic sensitivity reactions and should be avoided; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil or rivastigmine) are recommended by NICE and can improve hallucinations and cognition; levodopa may be used cautiously for motor symptoms.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: Alzheimer's disease presents with early episodic memory loss and gradual decline without prominent fluctuation, hallucinations or parkinsonism.
Correct: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism are the core features of dementia with Lewy bodies.
Incorrect: frontotemporal dementia causes early behavioural change, disinhibition or language impairment in younger patients.
Incorrect: normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive slowing without hallucinations or REM sleep disorder.
Incorrect: vascular dementia typically has a stepwise course with focal neurological signs and vascular risk factors.
learningPoint: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism indicate dementia with Lewy bodies; avoid antipsychotics and consider a cholinesterase inhibitor.

stem: A 28-year-old woman of Cypriot origin has a full blood count performed at a preconception check. She is asymptomatic, has regular light periods and eats a mixed diet. Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115–165), MCV 64 fL (80–100), MCH 20 pg (27–32), red cell count 5.9 x 10^12/L (3.8–5.8), red cell distribution width normal, ferritin 68 micrograms/L (15–200), CRP 2 mg/L (<5). The blood film shows microcytic hypochromic red cells with target cells and basophilic stippling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Beta thalassaemia trait (heterozygous beta thalassaemia) is common in people of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and South Asian origin and results from reduced or absent beta-globin chain synthesis from one allele. It produces a characteristic picture of mild or absent anaemia with disproportionately marked microcytosis and hypochromia, a raised or high-normal red cell count, a normal red cell distribution width (because the cells are uniformly small), and normal iron studies. The Mentzer index (MCV divided by red cell count) is below 13 in thalassaemia trait and above 13 in iron deficiency; here it is about 10.8. Target cells and basophilic stippling are typical film findings. In contrast, iron deficiency causes a low ferritin, a low red cell count and an increased red cell distribution width, and the MCV falls in proportion to the haemoglobin. The diagnosis is confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing raised HbA2 (above 3.5%), often with mildly raised HbF. No treatment is required, and iron should not be given unless there is coexisting deficiency. The key clinical implication is genetic counselling: if her partner also carries a beta (or certain other) thalassaemia or haemoglobin variant, there is a one in four chance of a child with thalassaemia major, so partner testing and antenatal screening (as in the NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme) are essential.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: anaemia of chronic disease is usually normocytic or mildly microcytic with a raised ferritin and inflammatory markers.
Correct: marked microcytosis with mild anaemia, raised red cell count, normal ferritin, target cells and stippling in a Mediterranean patient indicates beta thalassaemia trait.
Incorrect: iron deficiency would show a low ferritin, low red cell count and raised red cell distribution width.
Incorrect: lead poisoning causes basophilic stippling but with abdominal pain, neuropathy and exposure history, and is rare.
Incorrect: sideroblastic anaemia typically produces a dimorphic film with raised ferritin and ring sideroblasts in the marrow.
learningPoint: Disproportionate microcytosis with a raised red cell count, normal ferritin and Mentzer index below 13 suggests thalassaemia trait; confirm with raised HbA2 and offer partner screening.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of petechiae on her lower legs, spontaneous bruising and bleeding gums when brushing her teeth. She is otherwise well, has no fever, weight loss or night sweats, takes no medication and has no family history of bleeding. Examination shows petechiae and ecchymoses but no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Haemoglobin 132 g/L (115–165), white cell count 6.8 x 10^9/L (4–11), platelets 9 x 10^9/L (150–400). Blood film confirms marked thrombocytopenia with large platelets and no other abnormality. Coagulation screen, renal and liver function are normal; HIV and hepatitis C tests are negative. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
explanation: Primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder in which antiplatelet antibodies (often against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa) cause platelet destruction in the spleen and impair megakaryocyte platelet production. It is a diagnosis of exclusion based on isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal blood count and film, in the absence of other causes such as drugs, HIV, hepatitis C, lymphoproliferative disease or autoimmune conditions; bone marrow examination is not routinely required in a typical presentation. Treatment is indicated when the platelet count is below about 30 x 10^9/L or there is bleeding. First-line therapy is corticosteroids: either prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily tapered over several weeks, or high-dose dexamethasone 40 mg daily for four days. Intravenous immunoglobulin is used when a rapid rise is needed, for example with serious bleeding or before surgery, and is combined with steroids in emergencies. Platelet transfusion is ineffective except in life-threatening haemorrhage because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed. Second-line options for relapsed or refractory disease include thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab, fostamatinib and, less often now, splenectomy, which is deferred for at least 12 months from diagnosis because of the chance of spontaneous remission. Tranexamic acid helps mucosal bleeding and NSAIDs should be avoided.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: thrombopoietin receptor agonists are second-line agents for ITP that has relapsed or failed to respond to steroids.
Correct: corticosteroids (prednisolone or high-dose dexamethasone) are first-line treatment for newly diagnosed ITP with a count below 30 or bleeding.
Incorrect: transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed by the autoantibody and are reserved for life-threatening bleeding alongside steroids and IVIG.
Incorrect: rituximab is a second-line option after failure of corticosteroids.
Incorrect: splenectomy is reserved for chronic refractory ITP and deferred for at least 12 months.
learningPoint: Newly diagnosed ITP with platelets below 30 x 10^9/L or bleeding is treated first-line with corticosteroids; IVIG is added when a rapid response is needed.

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents with two days of confusion, headache, fever and a purpuric rash on her legs. She has no diarrhoea. Haemoglobin 84 g/L (115–165), platelets 14 x 10^9/L (150–400), white cell count 9.2 x 10^9/L (4–11), reticulocytes 6%, creatinine 142 micromol/L (60–110), LDH 1,650 U/L (<250), bilirubin 48 micromol/L (<21), direct antiglobulin test negative. Prothrombin time, APTT and fibrinogen are normal. The blood film shows numerous fragmented red cells and polychromasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
explanation: The combination of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (fragmented red cells, raised LDH and bilirubin, negative direct antiglobulin test) with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms, fever and mild renal impairment, in the presence of a normal coagulation screen, is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Acquired TTP is caused by autoantibodies against ADAMTS13, the protease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers; uncleaved multimers cause platelet-rich microthrombi in small vessels. Untreated mortality exceeds 90%, so treatment must begin as soon as the diagnosis is suspected on the basis of microangiopathic haemolysis and thrombocytopenia without another cause, without waiting for the ADAMTS13 activity result (which is sent before treatment and confirms the diagnosis if below 10%). Urgent plasma exchange with solvent-detergent plasma removes the antibody and replaces ADAMTS13, and is given daily until the platelet count normalises. High-dose corticosteroids are given alongside, and rituximab is now used early in acquired TTP. Caplacizumab, an anti-von Willebrand factor nanobody, is recommended by NICE as an adjunct. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated except for life-threatening bleeding because it fuels microvascular thrombosis. The normal clotting distinguishes TTP from disseminated intravascular coagulation, and the absence of diarrhoea and only modest renal impairment argue against haemolytic uraemic syndrome, in which renal failure dominates.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: renal impairment is mild and dialysis does not treat the underlying microangiopathy.
Incorrect: although sepsis should be considered, the microangiopathic picture with normal clotting indicates TTP, which antibiotics do not treat.
Incorrect: heparin has no role in TTP and would worsen bleeding risk with a platelet count of 14.
Correct: urgent plasma exchange is life-saving in TTP and must start as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.
Incorrect: platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP as it can precipitate further thrombosis and deterioration.
learningPoint: Microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and normal clotting is TTP until proven otherwise: start plasma exchange immediately and avoid platelet transfusion.

stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes an elective total hip replacement and receives prophylactic dalteparin from the day of surgery. His preoperative platelet count was 260 x 10^9/L (150–400). On postoperative day 7 he develops a swollen, painful left calf and Doppler ultrasound confirms an occlusive popliteal vein thrombosis. Platelets are now 78 x 10^9/L, haemoglobin 118 g/L, coagulation screen normal, and there is no bleeding, sepsis or other new medication. Skin at the injection sites is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue dalteparin at treatment dose and monitor platelets daily
Platelet transfusion and insertion of an inferior vena cava filter
Stop dalteparin and start warfarin alone
Switch to an unfractionated heparin infusion
explanation: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune-mediated adverse reaction in which IgG antibodies form against complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin, activating platelets via their Fc receptors and generating thrombin. It is paradoxically a prothrombotic state: venous or arterial thrombosis occurs in up to 50% of untreated cases, and bleeding is unusual. The typical onset is 5 to 10 days after starting heparin, with a platelet fall of more than 50% from baseline (often to a nadir of 20 to 100 x 10^9/L), and it is more common after orthopaedic surgery and with unfractionated than with low molecular weight heparin. The 4Ts score (thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes) estimates pretest probability; this patient scores highly. Management must not wait for laboratory confirmation (PF4 antibody immunoassay and functional assays): all heparin, including flushes and heparin-coated lines, is stopped immediately and a non-heparin anticoagulant started at therapeutic dose because of the thrombosis. Options are argatroban (a direct thrombin inhibitor, preferred in renal impairment), danaparoid, fondaparinux (off-label) or a direct oral anticoagulant. Warfarin must not be started until the platelet count has recovered above 150, because protein C depletion can precipitate venous limb gangrene; when introduced it must overlap with the parenteral agent. Platelet transfusion is avoided and heparin should be recorded as an allergy.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: continuing any heparin perpetuates the immune reaction and thrombosis risk.
Incorrect: platelet transfusion may worsen thrombosis in HIT and filters are not indicated when anticoagulation is possible.
Correct: stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban at treatment dose for confirmed thrombosis.
Incorrect: warfarin alone is contraindicated in acute HIT until platelets recover because of the risk of venous limb gangrene.
Incorrect: unfractionated heparin cross-reacts fully with HIT antibodies and is more likely to cause HIT than dalteparin.
learningPoint: A platelet fall of more than 50% five to ten days after heparin with new thrombosis indicates HIT: stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban; delay warfarin until platelets recover.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with three months of lower back pain, fatigue and two episodes of chest infection. Haemoglobin 96 g/L (130–180), MCV 92 fL (80–100), white cell count 5.1 x 10^9/L (4–11), platelets 190 x 10^9/L (150–400), ESR 105 mm/h (<20), adjusted calcium 2.86 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60–110), total protein 96 g/L (60–80), albumin 32 g/L (35–50). Blood film shows rouleaux. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates a monoclonal IgG kappa paraprotein of 38 g/L with suppression of the other immunoglobulins, and serum free light chains show an abnormal kappa:lambda ratio. Which investigation is required to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
Twenty-four hour urine collection for Bence Jones protein
explanation: This man has the classic features of symptomatic multiple myeloma, summarised by the CRAB criteria: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia and Bone lesions (back pain), together with recurrent infection from immune paresis, a high ESR, rouleaux and a large IgG kappa paraprotein. According to the International Myeloma Working Group criteria, the diagnosis of myeloma requires demonstration of clonal bone marrow plasma cells of 10% or more (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus at least one myeloma-defining event: a CRAB feature or a biomarker of malignancy (plasma cells 60% or more, involved:uninvolved free light chain ratio of 100 or more, or more than one focal lesion on MRI). The bone marrow aspirate and trephine therefore remains the confirmatory test, and also provides material for cytogenetics and FISH (for example del(17p), t(4;14) and t(14;16) confer high risk) that guide prognosis and treatment. NICE guidance (NG35) recommends whole-body MRI or, if unavailable, whole-body low-dose CT as first-line imaging for bone disease, having superseded the plain skeletal survey, which misses many lesions. Beta-2 microglobulin and albumin are used for staging (Revised International Staging System) rather than diagnosis. Urinary Bence Jones protein is largely replaced by serum free light chain assay. Initial management includes hydration, bisphosphonates, treatment of hypercalcaemia and referral for proteasome inhibitor-based induction therapy.
optionExplanations: Correct: demonstration of 10% or more clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow, with a CRAB feature, confirms multiple myeloma and provides cytogenetics.
Incorrect: the skeletal survey is insensitive and has been replaced by whole-body MRI or low-dose CT for detecting bone disease; it does not confirm diagnosis.
Incorrect: beta-2 microglobulin is a staging and prognostic marker, not a diagnostic test.
Incorrect: urinary light chain measurement has been largely superseded by serum free light chain assay and does not confirm marrow involvement.
Incorrect: imaging identifies bone lesions but cannot establish clonal plasma cell infiltration.
learningPoint: Myeloma is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing at least 10% clonal plasma cells plus a myeloma-defining event (CRAB or biomarker); whole-body MRI or low-dose CT has replaced the skeletal survey.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with fatigue, intermittent abdominal pain and passing dark brown urine, most noticeably first thing in the morning. One year ago he had a hepatic vein thrombosis with no provoking factor and a negative thrombophilia screen, and remains on warfarin. He also reports difficulty swallowing and erectile dysfunction. Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180), MCV 102 fL (80–100), reticulocytes 6% (0.5–2.5), platelets 98 x 10^9/L (150–400), neutrophils 1.4 x 10^9/L (2.0–7.5), LDH 1,200 U/L (<250), bilirubin 44 micromol/L (<21), haptoglobin undetectable, direct antiglobulin test negative, urinary haemosiderin positive. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Bone marrow cytogenetics for the JAK2 V617F mutation
Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 on red cells and granulocytes
explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired clonal disorder of haematopoietic stem cells caused by a somatic mutation in the PIGA gene, which is required for synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. Affected blood cells therefore lack all GPI-anchored surface proteins, including the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis), leaving red cells exposed to complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis. The classic triad is intravascular haemolysis (raised LDH, absent haptoglobin, haemoglobinuria that is often worse on waking because of nocturnal acidosis, negative direct antiglobulin test), thrombosis at unusual sites (hepatic, portal, mesenteric and cerebral veins; the leading cause of death) and cytopenias from associated bone marrow failure. Free haemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing smooth muscle dystonia with dysphagia, abdominal pain and erectile dysfunction. Diagnosis is by flow cytometry demonstrating populations of red cells and granulocytes deficient in GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59, or using the FLAER reagent, which binds GPI directly); this has replaced the historical Ham's test and sucrose lysis test. Treatment with terminal complement inhibitors (eculizumab or ravulizumab) abolishes intravascular haemolysis and dramatically reduces thrombosis, but requires prior meningococcal vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis. Allogeneic transplantation is curative and reserved for severe marrow failure.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: JAK2 mutations are found in myeloproliferative neoplasms, which cause splanchnic thrombosis but not intravascular haemolysis with cytopenias.
Correct: flow cytometry showing absent GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59 or FLAER) on red cells and granulocytes is the diagnostic test for PNH.
Incorrect: haemoglobin electrophoresis identifies haemoglobinopathies, which cause extravascular rather than intravascular haemolysis.
Incorrect: the Ham's test is the historical diagnostic test, now obsolete because it is insensitive and non-specific compared with flow cytometry.
Incorrect: osmotic fragility testing is used for hereditary spherocytosis, which is DAT-negative but has spherocytes and a family history.
learningPoint: Intravascular haemolysis with a negative DAT, unusual-site venous thrombosis and cytopenias suggests PNH; confirm by flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (CD55/CD59) and treat with complement inhibition.

stem: A 36-year-old man returned from a three-week business trip to Uganda ten days ago and did not take antimalarial chemoprophylaxis. He presents with three days of fever, rigors and headache, and today his wife has noticed he is drowsy. Temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius, heart rate 122/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 13. A thick and thin blood film shows Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitaemia of 8%. Glucose 2.9 mmol/L, creatinine 190 micromol/L (60–110), bilirubin 68 micromol/L (<21), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (0.5–2.2), platelets 42 x 10^9/L (150–400). Which is the most appropriate antimalarial treatment?
explanation: This man has severe falciparum malaria as defined by WHO criteria: impaired consciousness, hypoglycaemia, acute kidney injury, jaundice, raised lactate (metabolic acidosis), shock and a parasitaemia above 2% (in non-immune travellers, 2% or more is considered severe in UK guidance; above 10% is very high risk). Severe malaria is a medical emergency with a mortality of 10 to 20% even with treatment, and any patient with features of severity, or who cannot take oral medication, needs parenteral treatment on a high-dependency or intensive care unit. The UK malaria treatment guidelines (Lalloo et al., 2016, British Infection Association) recommend intravenous artesunate as the first-line agent, given at 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours and then daily, because the AQUAMAT and SEAQUAMAT trials showed it reduces mortality by around 22 to 35% compared with intravenous quinine and clears parasites faster with fewer adverse effects (quinine causes hypoglycaemia, arrhythmia and cinchonism). Intravenous quinine is used only if artesunate is unavailable. Once the patient can swallow and has improved, a full oral course of artemether-lumefantrine (or atovaquone-proguanil) completes treatment. Chloroquine has no role in falciparum malaria because of widespread resistance. Patients should be monitored for delayed haemolysis after artesunate (at day 14), hypoglycaemia, fluid balance, acidosis and secondary bacterial infection.
optionExplanations: Correct: intravenous artesunate is the first-line treatment for severe or complicated falciparum malaria and reduces mortality compared with quinine.
Incorrect: oral therapy is for uncomplicated malaria; a drowsy patient with organ dysfunction needs parenteral treatment.
Incorrect: atovaquone-proguanil is an oral option for uncomplicated falciparum malaria or follow-on therapy, not for severe disease.
Incorrect: chloroquine is ineffective against Plasmodium falciparum because of near-universal resistance.
Incorrect: oral quinine is a treatment for uncomplicated malaria; severe malaria with impaired consciousness requires intravenous therapy.
learningPoint: Severe falciparum malaria (impaired consciousness, acidosis, renal failure, hypoglycaemia, parasitaemia above 2%) is treated with intravenous artesunate, followed by a full oral course once improving.

stem: A 44-year-old man from Romania is six weeks into standard treatment for smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, together with pyridoxine 10 mg daily. He weighs 68 kg and takes no other medication. He attends clinic reporting two weeks of gradually worsening blurred vision in both eyes and difficulty distinguishing red from green when reading traffic lights, without eye pain. Visual acuity has fallen from 6/6 to 6/18 bilaterally and there is a central scotoma on Amsler grid testing; fundoscopy is normal. Liver function is normal. Which drug is most likely responsible for his visual symptoms?
explanation: Ethambutol causes a dose-related, usually reversible, retrobulbar optic neuropathy that presents with painless bilateral reduction in visual acuity, central or centrocaecal scotomas and loss of red-green colour discrimination, typically after two or more months of therapy but occasionally earlier. The risk is increased with doses above 15 to 20 mg/kg per day, in renal impairment (the drug is renally excreted), in older patients and with prolonged therapy. Fundoscopy is often normal initially because the lesion is behind the optic disc; later there may be optic atrophy. NICE tuberculosis guidance (NG33) and the BNF recommend documenting visual acuity (Snellen chart) and colour vision (Ishihara plates) before starting ethambutol, checking renal function to adjust the dose, and advising patients to stop the drug and report any visual change immediately. The drug should be stopped as soon as toxicity is suspected, and specialist ophthalmology review arranged; recovery may take months and is not universal, so early recognition is essential. In standard six-month therapy ethambutol is given only in the initial two-month phase. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine) and hepatitis and only very rarely optic neuritis; rifampicin causes orange discolouration of secretions including tears and can stain soft contact lenses, but does not affect acuity; pyrazinamide causes hepatitis, hyperuricaemia and arthralgia.
optionExplanations: Correct: ethambutol causes bilateral optic neuropathy with reduced acuity, central scotoma and red-green colour deficiency, requiring immediate withdrawal.
Incorrect: isoniazid classically causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis; optic neuropathy is very rare.
Incorrect: pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia and gout, not visual loss.
Incorrect: pyridoxine is given to prevent isoniazid neuropathy and does not cause visual symptoms at this dose.
Incorrect: rifampicin colours tears and body fluids orange and induces hepatic enzymes but does not impair acuity or colour vision.
learningPoint: Ethambutol causes reversible optic neuropathy with reduced acuity and red-green colour loss; check acuity and colour vision at baseline and stop the drug at the first visual symptom.

stem: A 38-year-old man who was diagnosed with HIV infection four years ago but has not engaged with care or taken antiretroviral therapy presents with three weeks of progressive exertional breathlessness, a dry cough and fevers. He has oral candidiasis. Respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturation 89% on air, which falls to 82% on walking. Arterial blood gas on air: PaO2 7.8 kPa (>10.6), PaCO2 4.1 kPa (4.7–6.0). Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates. CD4 count 68 cells/microlitre (500–1500), LDH 620 U/L (<250). Beta-D-glucan is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is the commonest AIDS-defining illness in patients presenting late with HIV, occurring almost exclusively when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/microlitre. The typical presentation is subacute progressive dyspnoea, dry cough and fever with marked exertional desaturation, a raised LDH and bilateral perihilar interstitial or ground-glass change on imaging; the chest radiograph may be normal early. Diagnosis is confirmed by immunofluorescence or PCR on induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage, with serum beta-D-glucan as a useful supportive marker. First-line treatment is high-dose co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim 15 to 20 mg/kg/day with sulfamethoxazole) for 21 days, given intravenously in severe disease. Crucially, patients with moderate to severe PCP, defined as a PaO2 below 9.3 kPa (70 mmHg) on air or an alveolar-arterial gradient above 4.7 kPa, should receive adjunctive corticosteroids (prednisolone 40 mg twice daily for 5 days, then 40 mg daily for 5 days, then 20 mg daily for 11 days) started within 72 hours of antimicrobial therapy, because they reduce the inflammatory deterioration that follows organism lysis and lower mortality and the need for ventilation. Alternatives for co-trimoxazole intolerance include clindamycin with primaquine, or intravenous pentamidine. Antiretroviral therapy should begin within two weeks, and secondary prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole continues until the CD4 count exceeds 200 for three months.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: co-trimoxazole is the right antimicrobial, but with a PaO2 below 9.3 kPa adjunctive steroids are required to reduce mortality.
Correct: high-dose co-trimoxazole plus prednisolone is indicated for moderate to severe PCP with hypoxaemia.
Incorrect: this regimen treats bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, which does not fit the subacute course, CD4 count and interstitial pattern.
Incorrect: amphotericin is used for cryptococcal or invasive fungal infections and is inactive against Pneumocystis.
Incorrect: fluconazole treats the oral candidiasis but has no activity against Pneumocystis jirovecii.
learningPoint: Treat PCP with high-dose co-trimoxazole for 21 days and add prednisolone within 72 hours if PaO2 is below 9.3 kPa on air; start antiretroviral therapy within two weeks.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents in July with a painless, slowly expanding red rash on her right thigh that she first noticed eight days ago. Three weeks earlier she spent a weekend walking and camping in the New Forest and recalls removing a small tick from the same area. The lesion is an oval erythematous patch 12 cm in diameter with partial central clearing, warm but not tender, with no scale. She has mild fatigue and headache but no fever, arthralgia, facial weakness, palpitations or neck stiffness. Examination is otherwise normal and she is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days
Send Lyme serology and treat only if positive
explanation: This is erythema migrans, the pathognomonic early localised manifestation of Lyme disease, caused by the spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi (in the UK mainly B. afzelii and B. garinii) and transmitted by Ixodes ticks in areas such as the New Forest, Exmoor, the Lake District and the Scottish Highlands. The rash appears 3 to 30 days after a tick bite as a slowly expanding erythematous patch, often more than 5 cm, sometimes with central clearing giving a target appearance; it is usually painless and non-itchy, distinguishing it from cellulitis or a hypersensitivity reaction, which appear within 48 hours and do not expand. NICE guidance (NG95) is explicit that erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis and antibiotics should be started without laboratory testing, because serology is frequently negative in the first few weeks before an antibody response develops and a negative test could falsely reassure. First-line treatment for adults is oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (or 200 mg once daily) for 21 days; amoxicillin for 21 days is the alternative in pregnancy or intolerance, and azithromycin is third-line. Intravenous ceftriaxone is reserved for Lyme disease with central nervous system involvement, and oral doxycycline is also used for Lyme arthritis, carditis and cranial nerve palsy. Patients should be advised about tick-bite prevention and that a Jarisch-Herxheimer-like reaction can occur early in treatment.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: intravenous ceftriaxone is for neuroborreliosis with central nervous system involvement, not uncomplicated erythema migrans.
Correct: erythema migrans is treated empirically with oral doxycycline for 21 days without waiting for serology.
Incorrect: flucloxacillin treats staphylococcal cellulitis, which is rapidly progressive, painful and does not have a slowly expanding target appearance.
Incorrect: serology is often negative in early Lyme disease and NICE advises treating erythema migrans on clinical grounds.
Incorrect: a slowly expanding non-scaly patch after a tick bite is not a fungal infection; tinea would be scaly with an active edge.
learningPoint: Erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis: treat with oral doxycycline for 21 days without serology, which is unreliable in early Lyme disease.

stem: A 73-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels eight times in 24 hours, with lower abdominal cramps, eight days after completing a course of co-amoxiclav for a urinary tract infection. She has never had similar symptoms before. Temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, abdomen soft with mild tenderness and no distension. White cell count 14.2 x 10^9/L (4–11), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60–110; baseline 80), albumin 34 g/L (35–50). Stool tests positive for Clostridioides difficile glutamate dehydrogenase antigen and toxin. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days
Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 10 days
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days
explanation: Clostridioides difficile infection follows disruption of the colonic microbiome by antibiotics, particularly broad-spectrum penicillins, cephalosporins, clindamycin and fluoroquinolones, allowing toxin-producing C. difficile to proliferate. Diagnosis uses a two-step algorithm (glutamate dehydrogenase antigen or PCR followed by toxin detection). Severity is assessed using markers such as a white cell count above 15 x 10^9/L, a creatinine rise of more than 50% above baseline, temperature above 38.5, or radiological or clinical evidence of severe colitis; this woman has a mild to moderate first episode. NICE guidance (NG199, 2021) changed UK practice: oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is now first-line for a first episode of any severity, because it is more effective than metronidazole, which is relegated to third-line use when vancomycin and fidaxomicin are unavailable. Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days is second-line if vancomycin is ineffective, and is the first-line option for a recurrence within 12 weeks because it reduces relapse rates. Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen and is useless. Life-threatening disease is treated with high-dose oral vancomycin plus intravenous metronidazole and surgical review. Faecal microbiota transplantation is recommended for two or more recurrences. The precipitating antibiotic should be stopped and proton pump inhibitors reviewed, and antimotility agents avoided.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: faecal microbiota transplantation is reserved for recurrent infection after two or more episodes.
Incorrect: intravenous vancomycin does not penetrate into the colonic lumen and has no effect on C. difficile.
Incorrect: fidaxomicin is second-line for a first episode, or first-line for early recurrence.
Incorrect: metronidazole is now third-line because of inferior efficacy compared with vancomycin.
Correct: NICE recommends oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days as first-line treatment for a first episode of C. difficile infection.
learningPoint: First episode of C. difficile infection: oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is first-line; fidaxomicin is used for treatment failure or recurrence within 12 weeks.

stem: A 29-year-old man returns from a four-week visit to family in rural Bangladesh. He presents with nine days of fever that has risen in a stepwise pattern to 39.6 degrees Celsius, frontal headache, dry cough, vague abdominal discomfort and constipation. He took no pre-travel vaccinations. Heart rate 62/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg. Examination shows a coated tongue, faint salmon-coloured macules on the upper abdomen and 2 cm splenomegaly. White cell count 3.2 x 10^9/L (4–11), platelets 118 x 10^9/L (150–400), ALT 96 U/L (<40). Three malaria films and a rapid antigen test are negative. Blood cultures have been taken. Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?
explanation: This presentation is typical of enteric (typhoid or paratyphoid) fever caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi or Paratyphi: a stepwise rising fever in the first week after return from South Asia, headache, dry cough, abdominal symptoms with constipation being more common than diarrhoea in adults, relative bradycardia, rose spots, splenomegaly, and leucopenia with thrombocytopenia and mildly raised transaminases. Blood cultures are the mainstay of diagnosis (positive in 60 to 80% in the first week) and bone marrow culture is most sensitive; the Widal test is unreliable. Antimicrobial choice is dictated by resistance patterns. Fluoroquinolone resistance (reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility) is now near-universal in isolates from South Asia, and multidrug resistance to ampicillin, co-trimoxazole and chloramphenicol is common; extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid resistant also to third-generation cephalosporins has emerged in Pakistan since 2016. UK guidance therefore recommends that severe or hospitalised enteric fever acquired in South Asia is treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g daily for 10 to 14 days), while azithromycin is the preferred oral agent for uncomplicated disease and for XDR strains acquired in Pakistan, where a carbapenem may be needed for severe disease. Ciprofloxacin is only appropriate when the isolate is proven susceptible. Complications in the third week include intestinal haemorrhage and perforation. Dexamethasone is added for severe disease with shock or altered consciousness.
optionExplanations: Correct: intravenous ceftriaxone is the recommended empirical treatment for suspected enteric fever acquired in South Asia because of widespread fluoroquinolone and multidrug resistance.
Incorrect: aminoglycosides have poor intracellular penetration and are ineffective against Salmonella Typhi despite in vitro activity.
Incorrect: fluoroquinolone resistance is near-universal in South Asian typhoid isolates, so ciprofloxacin is not appropriate empirically.
Incorrect: co-trimoxazole resistance is widespread in multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi from South Asia.
Incorrect: doxycycline is not effective for enteric fever and is used for rickettsial infections, leptospirosis and brucellosis.
learningPoint: Stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, leucopenia and constipation after South Asian travel suggests typhoid; treat empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone (or azithromycin orally) because fluoroquinolone resistance is near-universal.

stem: A 71-year-old woman develops sudden right arm and leg weakness with difficulty finding words at 09:15 while eating breakfast with her husband, who calls an ambulance immediately. She arrives in the emergency department at 10:30. Her NIHSS score is 12, blood pressure 168/92 mmHg and capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; CT angiography shows no large vessel occlusion. She takes aspirin 75 mg for previous angina but no anticoagulant, has had no recent surgery or bleeding, and platelets and INR are normal. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg with labetalol before any other treatment
explanation: This woman has an acute ischaemic stroke with a disabling deficit and a clearly documented onset 75 minutes before arrival. NICE guidance (NG128) recommends intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (or tenecteplase) for patients with acute ischaemic stroke who present within 4.5 hours of known symptom onset, once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded by imaging and contraindications have been checked; benefit is time-dependent, so treatment should be given as quickly as possible with a door-to-needle target of under 60 minutes. Blood pressure must be below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis, which hers is, so no antihypertensive pre-treatment is needed; aggressive lowering of blood pressure in acute ischaemic stroke is otherwise harmful. Prior low-dose aspirin is not a contraindication. Mechanical thrombectomy is indicated in addition to thrombolysis for confirmed proximal anterior circulation large vessel occlusion within 6 hours (or up to 24 hours with favourable perfusion imaging), but her CT angiogram shows no large vessel occlusion. Aspirin 300 mg is given to all patients not thrombolysed, and to thrombolysed patients only after 24 hours once repeat imaging excludes haemorrhage. Therapeutic heparin has no role in acute ischaemic stroke. After thrombolysis she requires neurological observations, swallow assessment and admission to a hyperacute stroke unit.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: aspirin is withheld until 24 hours after thrombolysis and repeat imaging; giving it now would not be the most appropriate immediate step.
Correct: she is within the 4.5-hour window with a disabling deficit and no contraindications, so intravenous alteplase should be given without delay.
Incorrect: anticoagulation with heparin increases haemorrhagic transformation and does not improve outcome in acute ischaemic stroke.
Incorrect: her blood pressure is already below the 185/110 mmHg threshold for thrombolysis, and aggressive lowering worsens penumbral perfusion.
Incorrect: thrombectomy requires a demonstrated large vessel occlusion, which CT angiography has excluded.
learningPoint: Give intravenous thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of ischaemic stroke onset once haemorrhage is excluded and BP is below 185/110 mmHg; add thrombectomy only for proven large vessel occlusion.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with four days of progressive symmetrical weakness that began in his feet and now involves his thighs and hands, with tingling in his fingers and toes and lower back pain. Two weeks earlier he had a self-limiting diarrhoeal illness. Examination shows flaccid weakness (power 3/5 proximally in the legs, 4/5 in the arms), absent reflexes throughout, mild bilateral facial weakness and reduced vibration sense distally. Forced vital capacity is 3.9 L (predicted 4.8 L) and he can swallow safely. CSF: protein 1.2 g/L (<0.45), white cells 2 per microlitre, glucose normal. Nerve conduction studies show prolonged distal latencies and conduction block. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, most often the acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy subtype in Europe, typically triggered by a preceding infection; Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis is the classic antecedent, with molecular mimicry between lipo-oligosaccharide and peripheral nerve gangliosides.
